title: IT Threat Intel - IT Cybersecurity
description: Curated IT / enterprise cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_threatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: The Shai-Hulud npm worm is still spreading and now hunts 469 separate credential locations — 400+ packages, 1,300+ versions and roughly 2 billion monthly downloads in its blast radius
items.content_text: The self-propagating npm worm known as Shai-Hulud remains the single broadest live exposure in enterprise IT. The current wave began at 09:00 UTC on 4 August 2026, when a compromised maintainer identity was used to publish malicious versions of keyv 6.0.0, cacheable-request 13.0.20, cache-manager 7.2.10, flat-cache, file-entry-cache and hundreds of others. Wiz counted over 400 distinct packages; Singapore’s CSA put the figure at more than 1,300 affected versions representing roughly two billion monthly downloads, and JFrog later tracked the campaign across 1,700+ versions. The worm is not a vulnerability — nothing was flawed, packages were simply replaced — and that is why there is no CVE and no patch. It runs from a preinstall lifecycle hook, executes an obfuscated payload under the Bun runtime, harvests npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS/Azure/GCP keys, Kubernetes secrets and AI service keys, then uses any writable publishing token to push infected patch releases of every package that identity can reach. It also plants execution hooks in repository files such as .vscode/tasks.json and Claude Code hook configurations, and injects workflows to steal GitHub Actions secrets. Command-and-control addresses are pulled from an Ethereum smart contract rather than hardcoded, so takedowns of individual domains achieve little. On 3 September GitGuardian reported that the credential-scanning logic had grown from 189 paths to 469 — .env files, shell history, package-manager configs, CLI caches, CI/CD systems, IDE settings and AI tool configs. That is the real lesson: the operators are not breaking trust relationships, they are collecting the credentials already lying around in build environments and riding them onward.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (GitGuardian research); JFrog Security Research; Wiz; CSA Singapore
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign began 4 Aug 2026; expanded credential scope reported 3 Sep 2026

items.title: Wordfence blocked more than 440,000 exploit attempts against two WordPress plugins in a file-upload campaign now running at scale
items.content_text: Two unauthenticated file-upload flaws in widely installed WordPress plugins are under sustained attack. CVE-2026-14894 in Super Forms, rated CVSS 9.8, is a missing file-type validation issue: attackers post Base64-encoded PHP to /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php through the super_submit_form endpoint and drop a web shell. Exploitation began on 14 July 2026 and peaked on 18 August at more than 40,000 requests a day, with Wordfence blocking over 250,000 attempts in total; the fix is Super Forms 6.3.314. CVE-2026-32475 in Elementor Pro, disclosed through Patchstack in August and fixed in 4.2.2, is a validation bypass reached by submitting a form’s File Upload field as an array, which lands PHP files under /wp-content/uploads/elementor/forms/. Attacks on that one started 19 August and account for a further 190,000-plus blocked attempts. The combined total passed 440,000. This matters beyond marketing sites: WordPress instances are frequently run by a business unit rather than central IT, on infrastructure that still sits inside the corporate network or shares an identity provider, and a PHP web shell on such a host is a foothold like any other. The two campaigns are opportunistic and internet-wide, so exposure is a function of patch latency alone.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (Wordfence telemetry, Patchstack advisory)
_threatfeed.date_note: Super Forms attacks from 14 Jul 2026; Elementor Pro attacks from 19 Aug 2026; reported 4 Sep 2026

items.title: McKesson confirms a data breach through third-party applications as ShinyHunters claims 284 million records and sets a $55 million deadline
items.content_text: McKesson, one of the largest pharmaceutical distributors in the United States, confirmed on 31 August that unauthorised access to customer data occurred through third-party applications. The company discovered the incident on 25 August and says the exposure is limited to a subset of customers in its Oncology & Multispecialty and Medical-Surgical business units. The extortion group ShinyHunters listed McKesson on its leak site, claimed roughly 284 million customer records, and demanded approximately $55 million by 1 September. The claimed data set includes personally identifiable information, protected health information, treatment and prescription records, billing data, employee records and details of customer physicians and clinics. The record count is the attacker’s figure and has not been validated by McKesson or any independent party — treat it as a claim, not a finding. What is worth generalising is the entry point. ShinyHunters has spent 2026 working through third-party SaaS integrations rather than exploiting the target directly, which means the compromised asset is often an OAuth grant or an integration token that central IT never inventoried. McKesson says it has reasonable assurance there is no ongoing unauthorised activity in its systems. Any organisation with a large connected-app estate should read this as a prompt to enumerate what is authorised against its own tenants.

_threatfeed.source_name: SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Discovered 25 Aug 2026; confirmed 31 Aug 2026; attacker deadline 1 Sep 2026

items.title: An API key left in public JavaScript exposed 8.7 million Manchester Airports Group customer records — no exploit was required
items.content_text: Manchester Airports Group, operator of Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports, detected unauthorised access on 25 August 2026 and disclosed the breach on 27 August. Around 8.7 million customer records were affected, covering email addresses, phone numbers, postcodes and vehicle registration details from car-park bookings, lounge and Fast Track purchases and airport Wi-Fi registrations. Payment card data was not involved and flight operations were unaffected. The extortion group FulcrumSec contacted BleepingComputer on 30 August claiming responsibility and around 86 GB of data, including roughly 200,000 upcoming 2026 travel itineraries with passenger names, terminals, booking references and vehicle registrations. Their account of the method is the part every IT team should sit with: they say they found an API key for Iterable, MAG’s marketing-automation platform, embedded in publicly readable page JavaScript, and then simply called the API. MAG has declined to confirm the specifics, so treat the mechanism as claimed rather than established — but a client-side secret is a failure mode that requires no vulnerability, leaves no exploit signature and is invisible to every vulnerability scanner you own. MAG restricted system access, engaged external advisers, notified authorities, temporarily suspended online booking and refused the extortion demand. The residual risk to customers is high-quality phishing: knowing someone’s travel dates, terminal and car registration makes a convincing lure.

_threatfeed.source_name: IT Security Guru; Computing; TechTimes (BleepingComputer contact with FulcrumSec)
_threatfeed.date_note: Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 27–28 Aug 2026; attacker claim 30 Aug 2026

items.title: A four-month intrusion at Thomson Reuters’ C-Track court platform may have exposed Social Security numbers and sealed case material across a dozen jurisdictions
items.content_text: Thomson Reuters disclosed on 2 September 2026 that an unauthorised party had access to court files held in its C-Track case-management platform, run by its West Publishing unit, between 1 March and 29 June 2026. The intrusion was discovered on 30 June and courts were notified between 23 and 27 July, more than a month before public disclosure. Affected jurisdictions include Alabama, Kentucky, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee and Wyoming, plus the U.S. Virgin Islands, Minnesota and Ontario. The exposed data can include names, Social Security numbers, driver’s licence numbers, dates of birth, medical information and health-insurance details, and Thomson Reuters has said confidential, redacted or sealed material may have been affected. No total number of affected individuals has been published and no actor has been identified; North Dakota’s court system has confirmed an active criminal investigation. Twelve months of credit monitoring is being offered. For IT leaders outside the legal sector the transferable point is the four-month dwell time inside a hosted platform holding third-party regulated data. When you outsource a records system, you outsource the detection capability that protects it, and your contractual notification clock starts only when the vendor decides it has enough to tell you.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; Help Net Security
_threatfeed.date_note: Access 1 Mar – 29 Jun 2026; discovered 30 Jun; courts notified 23–27 Jul; disclosed 2 Sep 2026

items.title: PaperCut print-management servers were hit as zero-days, and the vendor had to ship a second patch a day after the first
items.content_text: PaperCut released an emergency patch on 27 August 2026 for two flaws in PaperCut NG and MF version 25 and earlier, then issued a second release on 28 August with additional hardening. CVE-2026-82078 is unsafe dynamic class loading in the database connection utilities that allows arbitrary Java bytecode execution; CVE-2026-81578 is an improper access control issue in the web management interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker change server configuration remotely. Huntress reported limited in-the-wild exploitation across two customer environments, where attackers ran Base64-encoded commands to enumerate user accounts and identify the operating system — early-stage reconnaissance rather than a finished intrusion. Huntress researchers separately reproduced a full pre-authentication chain from remote configuration takeover to code execution against PaperCut NG 25.0.11.75758. Print servers are a recurring target for good reason: they are frequently internet-exposed to support remote and branch printing, they run with high privilege on Windows, they are often excluded from the standard patch cadence because printing is treated as facilities rather than IT, and a compromise gives an attacker a trusted foothold that talks to nearly every endpoint in the estate. Anyone who applied only the first patch should apply Release 2 as well.

_threatfeed.source_name: Help Net Security (Huntress research)
_threatfeed.date_note: Patch 27 Aug 2026; Release 2 on 28 Aug 2026

items.title: Attackers are impersonating IT support over Microsoft Teams external chat, then relaying credentials to domain controllers
items.content_text: A coordinated social-engineering operation tracked as Spring Ring used external Microsoft Teams accounts to contact more than 150 employees across at least ten companies, working from 26 distinct attacker identities. The pretext is the oldest one in the book — an IT support contact about a problem with the user’s account — but the channel is what makes it work. Teams external collaboration is enabled by default in many tenants, the message arrives inside a sanctioned corporate tool rather than in email, and there is no attachment or link for a gateway to inspect. In the observed intrusions the operator talks the user into granting a remote session, then silently installs a malicious MSI package that carries Node.js and JavaScript implants for persistent command execution, and moves laterally toward domain controllers. Some chains escalated from voice phishing into NTLM relay attacks against the domain controller directly. There is no vulnerability here and nothing to patch: the whole sequence is legitimate software driven by a person who was persuaded. The practical controls are configuration and process rather than detection — restricting who can initiate external Teams chat, publishing a verification procedure staff can use when someone claims to be IT, and alerting on unexpected MSI installation and new remote-access tooling on user endpoints.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News ThreatsDay bulletin
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 3 Sep 2026

items.title: A phishing operation across 46 countries installs legitimate remote-management software instead of malware — and the United States is the top target
items.content_text: ANY.RUN linked 601 separate cases to a single campaign that phishes users into installing legitimate remote monitoring and management software, giving the operator hands-on access without ever deploying a recognisable malicious binary. Activity spans 46 countries, with 45% of observed cases in the United States; education, technology and government are the most-targeted sectors, followed by banking, finance and manufacturing. The lures are mundane and effective: Canada Revenue Agency tax forms, UPS and shipping notices, Adobe PDF prompts, U.S. Social Security Administration themes and invoices. The delivery infrastructure is deliberately disposable — researchers catalogued 425 kit URLs across 240 hosts, and 94% of those hosts were observed for a single day only, which makes domain blocklists close to useless against it. The reason this technique keeps working is that RMM tools are signed, allow-listed in most environments, and often already present because a managed service provider uses one. An endpoint running a second, unfamiliar RMM agent looks like an inventory anomaly rather than an incident, and few organisations monitor for that. The defensible position is to decide which RMM products are sanctioned in your estate and treat every other one as an alert, not as noise.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (ANY.RUN research)
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 3 Sep 2026

items.title: The ATF declares a “major incident” after Qilin lists it — and the segmentation that limited it is the story
items.content_text: The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives confirmed a cybersecurity incident after the Qilin ransomware group listed the agency on its leak site on 26 August 2026. ATF said the affected system operates separately from its enterprise network, that there is no indication the enterprise network, the eForms platform or other infrastructure were touched, and that the system was disconnected once the intrusion was found. Operations continued without disruption. The agency designated the event a “major incident” under federal reporting criteria, with the Justice Department coordinating the investigation. Qilin has not published screenshots, described the data or set a release timeline, so the extent of any theft is unverified. Reported as of 28 August, this is a contained event rather than an unfolding one — but that containment is the transferable lesson. A standalone system with no trust path into the enterprise network turned what could have been an agency-wide ransomware event into a single-host incident with no operational impact. Most organisations have equivalents: legacy applications, contractor-managed platforms, test environments and acquired infrastructure. The question worth asking is whether yours are genuinely isolated or merely undocumented, because those two states look identical on a network diagram and behave very differently during an intrusion.

_threatfeed.source_name: SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Qilin listing 26 Aug 2026; ATF confirmation reported 28 Aug 2026

items.title: A backdoor called “ted” hides inside the victim’s own recompiled HAProxy binary and reports the same version string as a clean build
items.content_text: Rapid7 Labs documented a previously undescribed Linux toolkit it calls ted, found embedded directly into trojanised HAProxy load balancers at two South Korean organisations in the automotive and media sectors. Rather than running as a separate process or module, the implant is compiled into HAProxy itself. It watches for requests to specific image paths to switch into command-and-control mode, erases its own commands from HAProxy’s connection counters, and filters visitors on User-Agent, URL pattern, referer and an operator key — only requests that clear all four checks receive a modified page. Everything else gets normal traffic. Rapid7 attributes the toolkit with medium confidence to North Korean state-sponsored activity based on overlaps with APT37, Lazarus and Kimsuky tradecraft, and suspects initial access through exposed Korean groupware portals. The detection problem is the reason this belongs on every enterprise’s radar regardless of geography: a recompiled HAProxy reports the same version string as a clean build, so package version checks, vulnerability scanners and inventory tools all report a healthy system. Rapid7 recommends independent network correlation, memory behavioural analysis and binary integrity checking, and has published six domains, file paths and two SHA-256 hashes for retrospective log review.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (Rapid7 Labs research)
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 4 Sep 2026

items.title: Attackers are running their payloads through the signed Node.js runtime, and Symantec has traced intrusions lasting four months
items.content_text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team documented a set of targeted intrusions in which the operators use the legitimate, signed node.exe runtime to execute malicious JavaScript, chaining it with PowerShell and standard command-line tools. As Symantec put it, the malicious code lives in interpreted scripts rather than in a binary, which means signature-based detection has nothing to match on and application-control policies that trust signed developer tooling let it through. The campaign has been visible since February 2026, with one Asian technology company compromised from 23 March to 25 July and a U.S. fintech organisation showing activity from 6 May onward; government departments, technology firms and hotels are also among the targets. GuidePoint Security separately reported compromises at more than 31 organisations across e-commerce, professional services and retail logistics. The payload set is broad — AdaptixC2, Cobalt Strike Beacon, a Rust backdoor called C2Looper, ModeloRAT, Mistic/MLTBackdoor, a Node.js build of AsukaStealer, EtherRAT, a .NET payload called GateKeeper and a malicious Chrome extension named NexShield. Several use EtherHiding, pulling command-and-control addresses from the Ethereum blockchain so infrastructure can be rotated without touching the implant. The uncomfortable implication is that a developer tool present on thousands of corporate laptops is now a fully capable execution environment for an intruder.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (Symantec and GuidePoint research)
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 3 Sep 2026; activity observed from Feb 2026

items.title: Sophos publishes the affiliate playbook behind The Gentlemen ransomware: median dwell time of two days, EDR killed, backups disabled first
items.content_text: Sophos’ Counter Threat Unit released an analysis of the ransomware-as-a-service operation known as The Gentlemen, which it tracks as GOLD SHERWOOD. The group’s first leak-site victims appeared in September 2025 and the pace has accelerated sharply: 683 victims listed through July 2026, with 169 of those added in July alone. Initial access is unglamorous and familiar — exploitation of firewall vulnerabilities, notably CVE-2024-55591 in FortiGate devices, and abuse of VPN credentials, including one case where the affiliate simply authenticated to a Fortinet SSL VPN with valid credentials and no multi-factor protection. From there the affiliates escalate privileges using native Windows utilities to manipulate group membership, stage tools in the legitimate C:\PerfLogs directory, scan with Advanced IP Scanner and SoftPerfect, and exfiltrate with Rclone. Before encrypting, they deploy a custom EDR-killing toolkit called GentleKiller alongside bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver techniques, disable backup services including VeeamBackupSvc, SQLWriter and BackupExecAgent using sc config, and clear Application, System and Security event logs across multiple hosts. Median dwell time is around two days, and in some intrusions ransomware landed within 24 hours of initial access. The defensive read: MFA on every VPN path, tamper protection on EDR, backup services monitored for state changes, and log forwarding off-host so clearing them locally achieves nothing.

_threatfeed.source_name: Sophos Counter Threat Unit; reported via The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 3 Sep 2026; victim data through July 2026

items.title: Microsoft details a phishing operation that sent up to 2.37 million messages a day using invisible Unicode to break keyword filters
items.content_text: Microsoft Security Research documented a high-volume phishing campaign that defeated keyword-based email filtering with a simple trick: inserting invisible Unicode tag characters from the U+E0000–U+E007F range inside financial keywords. A filter looking for the literal string “funding” sees a fragmented token and passes the message; the recipient sees ordinary text, because the characters render as nothing. Volumes ran between one and 2.37 million messages on weekdays, peaking on 26 February 2026, with a clear weekday cadence and weekend dormancy, and a high-volume phase from early February through mid-May before dropping off sharply. The lures targeted Small Business Administration loan applicants with offers of business loans, credit lines and advance funding, routing clicks through a legitimate marketing platform’s click-tracking infrastructure to hundreds of disposable finance-themed domains. Notably, the goal was not credential theft but the collection of detailed business and financial information to feed later spear-phishing. Fortra’s intelligence team had previously reported related SBA loan phishing activity. The technique generalises beyond this campaign: any control that matches on literal strings — email filters, data-loss-prevention rules, log-based detections — can be defeated by characters that carry no visual weight, and normalising Unicode before matching is the fix.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (Microsoft Security Research)
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 4 Sep 2026; campaign peak 26 Feb 2026

items.title: SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances are being attacked through two zero-days that chain into unauthenticated remote code execution
items.content_text: SonicWall published an advisory on 1 September 2026 and confirmed active exploitation of two flaws in its SMA 1000 secure access appliances. CVE-2026-83548 carries a CVSS of 10.0: a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets a remote unauthenticated attacker reach sensitive internal functionality. CVE-2026-83549, scored 7.8, is an OS command injection in the Appliance Management Console that normally requires administrator authentication. Chained, the SSRF supplies the access the command injection needs, and the result is unauthenticated code execution on the appliance. Affected models are the SMA 1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v on versions 12.4.3-03453 and earlier and 12.5.0-02835 and earlier; the fixed builds are 12.4.3-03526 and 12.5.0-02952. CISA added both to the KEV catalog on 2 September with a federal remediation deadline of 5 September. Shadowserver counts roughly 400 internet-exposed SMA 1000 appliances worldwide, some of which may already be patched — a small population, but one composed almost entirely of enterprises, government bodies and critical-infrastructure operators using the device as their remote-access boundary. This is also the third SMA 1000 exploitation event in recent memory, following CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410 in July, which UTA0533 used to deploy KNUCKLEBALL malware. SonicWall’s own guidance is unusually direct: if you find indicators of compromise, re-image the appliance and replace credentials and TOTP seeds rather than cleaning it.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; BleepingComputer; Rapid7 (SonicWall advisory, Shadowserver exposure data)
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisory 1 Sep 2026; reported 2 Sep 2026; KEV listing 2 Sep 2026

items.title: Google patches the sixth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026 — a V8 type confusion reachable from a crafted web page
items.content_text: Google shipped a Chrome update on 4 September 2026 fixing CVE-2026-85046, a type-confusion flaw in the V8 JavaScript engine rated CVSS 8.8, and confirmed that an exploit exists in the wild. The advisory language is the standard formulation: type confusion in V8 in Chrome prior to 152.0.7977.82 allowed a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page. Fixed builds are 152.0.7977.82/.83 on Windows and macOS and 152.0.7977.82 on Linux, and the release contains 12 security fixes in total. Researcher Salvatore Gulizia reported the bug on 4 August 2026; his description is that a compiler bug causes an array holding PACKED_ELEMENTS to receive the PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS map, which converts into arbitrary read and write on the JavaScript heap. Google has withheld attack details while users patch, which is normal practice and means there is currently no public information on who is being targeted. Two things are worth keeping in proportion. The execution is inside the renderer sandbox, so a full compromise requires a second bug to escape it — this is one stage of a chain, not instant device takeover. But Chrome and Chromium-derived browsers are on essentially every corporate endpoint, browser updates frequently stall on machines that are never restarted, and this is the sixth exploited Chrome zero-day this year. Force the restart.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; BleepingComputer (Google Chrome release advisory)
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported by researcher 4 Aug 2026; patched and disclosed 4 Sep 2026

items.title: Seven new KEV entries, five due 5 September — and four of them are developer or AI platform components
items.content_text: CISA added seven vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September 2026. Alongside the two SonicWall SMA 1000 flaws covered separately, the batch includes CVE-2026-9586, an SQL injection in Sangoma Switchvox scored 9.3; CVE-2026-82329, an improper-authentication flaw in JFrog Artifactory at 9.8; CVE-2026-48710, an HTTP request-smuggling issue in the Starlette Python framework at 6.5, reported as chained with CVE-2026-42271; CVE-2026-49869, an OS command injection in Kestra OSS at 10.0; and CVE-2026-59822, an improper-authentication flaw in Berri LiteLLM at 8.8. Federal remediation deadlines are 5 September for five entries and 16 September for the Starlette and LiteLLM items. The observed exploitation is instructive: attackers used the Switchvox and Artifactory flaws to open reverse shells and mint administrative tokens for enumeration, used the Kestra flaw to establish a reverse shell, enumerate the Docker container environment and deploy a cryptocurrency miner, and used the LiteLLM flaw to deliver an XMRig miner alongside credential theft and persistence. That is four of seven sitting in build, orchestration and AI-gateway infrastructure — systems that are usually internal-facing, thinly authenticated, excluded from EDR coverage and holding registry or cloud credentials. If your vulnerability programme scopes only servers and endpoints, this batch will not appear in it at all.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (CISA KEV catalog additions)
_threatfeed.date_note: KEV listing 2 Sep 2026; reported 3 Sep 2026

items.title: A NetScaler flaw Citrix called a denial of service turned out to be unauthenticated RCE — and it is now being exploited with web shells
items.content_text: Citrix patched CVE-2026-8452 on 30 June 2026, describing it as a memory-overflow condition affecting NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as AAA virtual servers or Gateway VPN servers. On 14 August, WatchTowr published a proof of concept demonstrating that the flaw is exploitable for unauthenticated remote code execution, materially worse than the vendor’s original characterisation. Exploitation in the wild followed shortly after, observed by Previdian (formerly KEVIntel) and Defused: 36 attempts across 12 days from 12 unique IP addresses in 10 countries, with attackers deploying web shells named x.php and z.php and running discovery commands such as id and echo. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 26 August with a federal deadline of 29 August. Fixed builds include 14.1-72.61 (FIPS), 13.1-63.18 and 13.1-37.272. NetScaler sits at the authentication boundary for remote access in a very large number of enterprises, and this pattern — a two-month gap between a low-drama vendor advisory and public weaponisation — is exactly how appliances end up unpatched. If you deferred the June update because the impact statement said denial of service, the appliance has now been exploitable for three weeks and needs a compromise assessment, not just a patch.

_threatfeed.source_name: SecurityWeek; The Hacker News; Help Net Security
_threatfeed.date_note: Patched 30 Jun 2026; PoC 14 Aug; exploitation observed from mid-Aug; KEV 26 Aug 2026

items.title: Nearly 22,000 on-premises Exchange servers are still exposed to a critical authentication bypass, and a working exploit is circulating
items.content_text: CVE-2026-62911 is a critical authentication-bypass flaw in Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019, scored CVSS 8.0, that allows an attacker to elevate privileges over the network via capture-replay. Microsoft patched it on 11 August 2026; it was reported by Orange Tsai of DEVCORE working with Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative. Three weeks later, Shadowserver’s daily scans counted close to 22,000 unpatched internet-facing servers — roughly 6,200 in the United States and 5,100 in Germany, where the federal BSI assessed that around 85% of on-premises Exchange servers in the country remain vulnerable. NCSC-NL in the Netherlands confirmed on 2 September that a working exploit is now circulating publicly. There is no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation as of this edition, but the combination of a public exploit, an enormous unpatched population and a target that historically attracts mass exploitation within days is about as clear a warning as this catalogue produces. Exchange also carries an unusual multiplier: it holds mail for the whole organisation, it is deeply integrated with Active Directory, and privilege escalation on the Exchange server has repeatedly been the first step toward domain compromise. Exchange 2016 and 2019 are out of mainstream support, so Extended Security Updates enrolment is required to receive the fix at all — which is a large part of why so many servers remain unpatched.

_threatfeed.source_name: Help Net Security (Shadowserver scan data, NCSC-NL and BSI advisories)
_threatfeed.date_note: Patched 11 Aug 2026; exposure and exploit circulation reported 2 Sep 2026

items.title: A CVSS 9.8 flaw in Cisco Nexus 9000 switches exposes two TCP ports that hand an unauthenticated attacker root
items.content_text: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-20212 on 2 September 2026, a CVSS 9.8 remote code execution flaw in the Silicon One component of specific Cisco Nexus 9000 series switches. The cause is a service bound to an unrestricted IP address, which leaves TCP ports 43210 and 43211 reachable; an unauthenticated attacker who can connect to them can send crafted input that executes with root privileges, or crash the S1HAL process and force a device reload. Affected models include the N9324C-SE1U, N9348Y2C6D-SE1U, N9364E-SG2-O and -SG2-Q, N9396T12C-SE1, N9348Y12C-SE1, N9396Y12C-SE1, N9336C-SE1, N9K-C9804 and N9K-C9808, across NX-OS releases 10.3(1) through 10.6(3s) — 45 releases in total. Cisco said it was not aware of malicious use at the time of disclosure. The remediation path is an upgrade to NX-OS 10.6(4) or later; where that cannot be scheduled quickly, Cisco offers an infrastructure access control list blocking ports 43210 and 43211, and a temporary Live Protect shield (lp00031) for 10.6(3) and 10.6(3s) only. Data-centre switches deserve a higher priority than their patch cadence usually reflects. Root on the fabric means traffic interception, configuration change and a position that most segmentation models never anticipated an attacker holding — and these particular models are concentrated in high-throughput and AI data-centre builds, where a forced reload is itself a serious availability event.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-n9k-s1-rce-EH8dEtr)
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisory published 2 Sep 2026

items.title: A CVSS 9.8 Gitea remote code execution flaw entered KEV within days — and open registration is what makes it unauthenticated in practice
items.content_text: CVE-2026-60004 is a remote code execution flaw affecting Gitea 1.17 and every release since, fixed in 1.27.1 and rated CVSS 9.8. The mechanism is that Gitea’s diffpatch endpoint can be abused to install and execute a Git hook from repository-controlled content. Technically the flaw requires write access to a repository, which sounds like a meaningful barrier — but Gitea enables open registration by default, so on a default deployment anyone reachable on the network can create an account, create a repository and reach the vulnerable path without any prior authorisation. The issue was reported by researcher Shai Rod (NightRang3r). CISA added it to KEV on 25 August 2026 with a federal deadline of 28 August, and a developer publicly documented an attack on their own Gitea instance in which the payload behaved like a cryptominer dropper: it cleared environment variables, looked for high-CPU processes, tried to kill competitors, fetched an architecture-specific payload, executed it and deleted its traces. Self-hosted Git servers are a common shadow-IT artefact — stood up by a team that wanted somewhere to keep code, never registered with central IT, and holding CI credentials, deployment keys and proprietary source. The realistic first step here is not patching but discovery.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (CISA KEV, researcher disclosure)
_threatfeed.date_note: KEV listing 25 Aug 2026; federal deadline 28 Aug 2026

items.title: ServiceNow patches three CVSS 10.0 flaws in its AI Platform, all reachable without authentication or user interaction
items.content_text: ServiceNow published fixes on 27 August 2026 for four flaws in its AI Platform, three of them scored CVSS 10.0. CVE-2026-18885 is a code-injection issue in the GraphQL Composite Data API that allows an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code and read or modify instance data. CVE-2026-18886 is an improper access control problem in the configuration image-upload processor permitting unauthenticated privilege escalation through data creation and modification. CVE-2026-74820 is a SQL injection reached through a dynamic schema ORDER BY clause, allowing arbitrary SQL against the backend database. A fourth, CVE-2026-6876 at CVSS 8.7, is a sandbox escape enabling unauthenticated code execution within the Now Platform. All three maximum-severity flaws share the same CVSS vector: network attack, no privileges, no user interaction, high impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. Affected releases span Xanadu before Patch 11 Hot Fix 7a, Yokohama before Patch 12 Hot Fix 3b and Patch 13 Hot Fix 4, several Zurich patch levels through Patch 12, and Australia before Patch 5. ServiceNow reported no awareness of exploitation as of 28 August and no public exploits exist. The reason to act anyway is what a ServiceNow instance contains: asset inventories, change records, privileged-access requests, incident history and often credentials embedded in workflow integrations. It is a map of the enterprise, and unauthenticated read access to it is valuable long before anyone runs code.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (ServiceNow security advisories)
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisories published 27 Aug 2026

items.title: PostgreSQL fixes a 12-year-old logical-decoding behaviour that lets a replication role execute code as the database operating-system user
items.content_text: The PostgreSQL project has patched CVE-2026-6471, nicknamed PostGREShell, a CVSS 7.2 flaw present since logical decoding was introduced in PostgreSQL 9.4 in 2014. An account holding the REPLICATION attribute, on a server configured with wal_level = logical, can execute arbitrary code as the operating-system user running the database. The cause is that the plugin name supplied in a CREATE_REPLICATION_SLOT command is passed straight to the library-loading function, and path-traversal characters and filesystem separators are accepted inside double-quoted plugin names — so an attacker can load any library on the host rather than only approved output plugins. Fixed releases are 18.6, 17.11, 16.15, 15.19 and 14.24, and the fix introduces a new output_plugin_libraries parameter that whitelists permitted plugins, defaulting to pgoutput, test_decoding. As of 4 September there is no public proof-of-concept and the flaw is not in KEV. The reason it earns a place here despite requiring a privileged role is that REPLICATION is routinely handed out far more freely than its impact warrants — to change-data-capture pipelines, analytics connectors, monitoring agents and managed replication tooling, often as a shared credential in a configuration file. Any of those becoming code execution on the database host is a serious escalation.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; SecurityWeek (PostgreSQL project advisory)
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 4 Sep 2026

items.title: Eleven further KEV additions in the last week of August, including four flaws from 2015, 2019, 2021 and 2022
items.content_text: Beyond the entries covered separately, CISA added a run of exploited vulnerabilities between 24 and 27 August 2026. On 24 August came CVE-2026-21962, an improper access control flaw in Oracle HTTP Server and WebLogic. The 26 August batch of six paired the Citrix NetScaler flaw with CVE-2019-1068 in Microsoft SQL Server and four older issues linked to activity tracked as UAT-10147 against Windows and Linux servers: CVE-2022-0995, an out-of-bounds write in the Linux kernel; CVE-2015-5287, a symlink privilege escalation in Red Hat ABRT; CVE-2015-3246, a race condition in Red Hat libuser; and CVE-2021-23758, a deserialisation flaw in Ajax.NET Professional. Federal deadlines were 29 August for the first two and 9 September for the four legacy entries. On 27 August three more followed: CVE-2023-49105, a CVSS 9.8 improper-authentication flaw in ownCloud Server 10.6.0–10.13.0 that lets an unauthenticated attacker who knows a username read, alter or delete files when no signing key is configured; CVE-2026-53362, a CVSS 7.8 out-of-bounds write in the Linux kernel IPv6 subsystem; and CVE-2026-66384, a CVSS 5.3 path traversal in JFrog Artifactory’s Docker cache handling. The through-line is that four of these are between four and eleven years old. Attackers are not short of new vulnerabilities — they are exploiting the ones that were never remediated because the risk register scored them low years ago.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; SecurityAffairs; Infosecurity Magazine (CISA KEV catalog)
_threatfeed.date_note: KEV listings 24, 25, 26 and 27 Aug 2026

items.title: EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations start on 11 September — 24 hours to tell ENISA about an actively exploited vulnerability in your product
items.content_text: Article 14 of the EU Cyber Resilience Act takes effect on 11 September 2026, and it applies to any manufacturer placing a product with digital elements on the EU market, whether or not they are established in the EU. Two triggers start the clock: becoming aware that a vulnerability in your product is being actively exploited, or discovering a severe incident affecting the product’s security. The deadlines are an early warning to ENISA and the relevant national CSIRT within 24 hours, a fuller notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days for vulnerabilities or one month for severe incidents. Reporting goes through the ENISA Single Reporting Platform, which currently requires manual form completion with no API. Several scope details matter in practice: the obligation continues after a product is no longer supported, vulnerabilities in third-party components must be reported if they are exploitable within your product, there is no retroactive reporting for anything discovered before 11 September, and users must be notified with disclosure proportional to risk. Exemptions cover medical devices, defence products and SaaS. Penalties reach €15 million or 2.5% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher, plus possible recalls. If your organisation ships software, firmware, an app or a connected device into Europe, the practical question this week is who holds the pager for a 24-hour regulatory clock.

_threatfeed.source_name: Pearl Cohen; Crowell & Moring (EU Cyber Resilience Act Article 14)
_threatfeed.date_note: Analysis published 31 Aug 2026; obligations begin 11 Sep 2026

items.title: A stopgap funding bill keeps the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act alive to 11 December — the fourth short extension in a year
items.content_text: The House passed a continuing resolution on 1 September 2026 that funds the government to 11 December 2026 and, in doing so, extends the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 past its 30 September sunset to the same date. The law provides liability protection to private-sector organisations that voluntarily share cyber threat indicators with federal agencies including CISA and NSA, and it is the legal basis on which a great deal of routine industry-to-government and ISAC sharing rests. The same bill temporarily extends the Technology Modernization Fund and the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act, both of which were also due to expire on 30 September. Efforts at a permanent reauthorisation have stalled repeatedly over the past year despite broad support from industry and officials, leaving the protections to be renewed in short increments attached to funding legislation. For security leaders the practical consequence is planning uncertainty rather than immediate change: sharing programmes continue to operate, but the legal protection underpinning them now has a horizon measured in weeks. If your threat-sharing arrangements, ISAC membership terms or vendor contracts reference these protections, it is worth knowing where the dependency sits before the next deadline rather than after it.

_threatfeed.source_name: Defense One
_threatfeed.date_note: House passage 1 Sep 2026; new sunset 11 Dec 2026

items.title: CISA still expects to finalise the CIRCIA incident-reporting rule this month — 72 hours for incidents, 24 hours for ransom payments
items.content_text: CISA has targeted September 2026 for publication of the final rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022. As proposed, covered entities in critical-infrastructure sectors would have to report substantial cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours and any ransom payment within 24 hours. The rule has slipped repeatedly: the statutory deadline was October 2025, CISA’s own prior internal target was May 2026, and the agency held town-hall consultations in June 2026 with more than 1,200 participants before settling on the current timeline. Final thresholds for who counts as a covered entity — based on sector and size criteria set out in the April 2024 proposed rule — remain pending, which is precisely the detail most organisations need in order to know whether they are in scope. Carried here as still-current rather than new: the September target was set in July and had not been superseded as of this edition. The reason to prepare regardless of the publication date is that a 72-hour clock is short if nobody has decided in advance who declares an incident reportable, who writes the report and who signs it. Organisations that already report under NIS2, DORA, SEC disclosure rules or state regulations should be mapping CIRCIA against those obligations now rather than building a separate process.

_threatfeed.source_name: Hunton Andrews Kurth privacy and cybersecurity blog (CISA regulatory agenda)
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 17 Jul 2026; final rule targeted for September 2026
